entities.name: Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, adopted on July 17, 1998, in Rome, Italy, represents a landmark treaty in international law that established the ICC as the first permanent international court dedicated to prosecuting individuals for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. Its creation was driven by a collective desire to end impunity for the perpetrators of the gravest crimes known to humanity, with significant contributions from key figures such as former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan and various national leaders who recognized the need for a robust judicial mechanism to address atrocities.

The statute entered into force on July 1, 2002, after receiving the required 60 ratifications, with the first case being brought to the ICC in 2004 against Thomas Lubanga Dyilo for the war crimes committed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The court operates on the principle of complementarity, meaning it intervenes only when national courts are unwilling or unable to prosecute serious crimes, thus promoting accountability while respecting national sovereignty. Over 120 countries have ratified the statute, showcasing a global commitment to international justice and the rule of law.

The legacy of the Rome Statute is profound, influencing the development of international criminal law and fostering cooperation among nations to combat impunity. Its establishment marked a shift in how the international community addresses human rights violations, inspiring subsequent treaties and legal frameworks aimed at protecting victims and prosecuting offenders. The ICC has faced challenges, including criticisms regarding its effectiveness and accusations of bias, yet it remains a symbol of the international community's efforts to uphold justice and deter future atrocities.
